She took Graham’s arm and they all walked very slowly. “We’re going to be late,” Matthew said worriedly. “Just fashionably late,” Audra said. “I tell you, these shoes looked so cute online! Who knew they’d be impossible to walk in?” Graham and Matthew exchanged a look—the shared knowledge that it would be wiser not to answer that.'

Title: Shuggie Bain
Author: Douglas   Stuart
My Review:
I read Shuggie in three hours during a sleepless night (in retrospect, it probably exacerbated my insomnia rather than curing it.) This novel is relentless.

The setting and situation—a crowded tenement apartment in 1980s Glasgow—is bleak when Shuggie begins, and things get bleaker. And bleaker. And bleaker.

If you can stand the emotional flagellation, Shuggie will reward you. The characterization is excellent; I understood each character's motivations, weaknesses, and quirks in sometimes painful clarity. The writing is intentional and strangely beautiful—strangely because so often, what's being described is ugly. There's an intimacy with poverty and addiction that rings true.

I agree with other reviewers: Shuggie isn't a great pick if you're struggling. But if you can bear it, you'll fall in love with this book.

Title: We Keep the Dead Close: A Murder at Harvard and a Half Century of Silence
Author: Becky Cooper
My Review:
If you enjoyed I'll Be Gone in the Dark by Michelle McNamara, We Keep The Dead Close is a brilliant campanion.

Like McNamara, Becky Cooper is a talented writer and journalist. She brings you with her to Harvard's campus, teeming with secrets and tradition; archaeological digs and explorations; and at one point, even Hawaii. Cooper is revisiting the places her subject, Jane Britton, once lived before her murder. Every location has echoes of Jane's past.

Cooper identifies strongly with Jane, but she's still enigmatic. I'd love to read a standalone memoir from Cooper—she feels like a fascinating friend who always exits the party before you’ve gotten a chance to really talk.

Title: Luster
Author: Raven Leilani
My Review:
Luster is the most gripping book I've read in a long time.

Like other reviewers, I picked it up for a bit of casual reading—and found myself, two hours later, still in the same place, gorging myself on Raven Leilani's prose.

I've read other unputdownable books before. However, these are usually suspense/thrillers, like Gone Girl.

The plot isn't "the thing" in Luster. The plot is a vehicle for Leilani's commentary on race, class, urban life vs. suburbia, sex, sex in the workplace, sex as a stand-in for power, family dynamics, and more. Rattling that list off, you might wonder if Luster is overwhelming or didactic. It's not. These strands are woven together almost seamlessly.

Leilani's run-on sentences lull you to sleep and then kick you in the ribs. This book has stunning power. It's hard to believe it's a debut.

Title: Akin
Author: Emma Donoghue
My Review:
I loved *Room*, so I was excited for *Akin*—although the book blurb told me this was going to be a different type of read.

Unfortunately, *Akin* was nowhere near as compelling. I found myself frequently rolling my eyes at the complaints and stodginess of the near-octogenarian (he's 79 for a few more weeks) Noah. He half-volunteers, half-capitulates to a trip to Nice, France, with his 11-year-old grand-nephew, Michael. The boy is from a dangerous neighborhood in Harlem, as we're reminded many, many times.

As one can imagine, the pair doesn't get along famously. Generational and class disparities cause sparks to fly, exacerbated by the cultural differences between the States and France. Of course, the boy eventually causes the old man's heart to melt, yadi yadi ya... Despite the predictability of this plot line, it was the only part I was interested by. There's an awkward sub-plot about Noah's mother (was she a Nazi informant or a hero of the Resistance?) as well as another, equally awkward, sub-plot about Mike's mom (is she a martyr or a drug addict?)

It felt like a fever dream where NCIS meets All the Light We Cannot See meets A Man Called Ove.

Title: The Body Politic
Author: Brian Platzer
My Review:
The Body Politic has all the ingredients of a novel I typically love: set in modern-day Manhattan, character-driven, morally ambiguous, and elegantly written.

Needless to say, I had high expectations. This book fulfilled them.

It never lost my attention; in fact, I only became more engrossed as I was pulled deeper into the fortunes (and misfortunes!) of the four friends. I saw myself in all of them—I think most readers will.

As other reviewers have noted, The Body Politic can be tough to read, especially as our nation battles a pandemic, racial injustice, and widespread class tension. It's like facing yourself in the mirror after a rough night. Not fun, but necessary.

4.5/5 stars

Disappearing Earth deserves the hype.

The first chapter did nothing to ease my anxiety; the language was evocative and beautiful (a constant throughout) but the plot had undertones of Gone Girl. Fortunately, the airport thriller vibes vanished—ha—in Chapter Two. This book might begin with the abduction of two girls, but it's really about the interconnected lives of the residents of Petropavlovsk, in Kamchatka Krai, Russia.

Before Disappearing Earth, I knew nothing about Kamchatka, let alone Petropavlovsk. Phillips paints a wonderfully layered picture of a region divided by tensions between modernity and tradition, indigeneity and inheritance.

Switching narrators every chapter was a little jarring, at first, and I had to flip back frequently to the catalogue of characters. Midway through the book, however, I started recognizing people from mentions in earlier sections. The initial confusion is worth the pay-off of the intricate web of relationships, and Phillips does an excellent job giving each narrator a distinct voice.

Disappearing Earth's length belies its punch. This book will stay with me a long time.

Title: Open Book
Author: Jessica Simpson
My Review:
Update:

After reading some of Open Book's glowing reviews, I decided to give this a second chance.

What I liked:

- Simpson's honesty: This reads like a classic addiction memoir; she's holding nothing back.
- The pace: It moves fairly quickly, going from her childhood as an aspiring star to one of the biggest names on Earth in just ten or so chapters.

What I didn't like:

- The language: My initial take (VV) still feels pretty accurate.

I know lots of people who aren't typical celebrity memoir readers really liked Open Book, but I'd steer you away unless you're a big fan of Simpson's and/or a pop culture fanatic.

Original review:

I couldn’t get past the first chapter. This was SO poorly written—it’s like Simpson spoke her thoughts into an recorder and then published them wholesale.

There’s zero trace of an editor, which means we get lots of abrupt transitions, total non sequiturs, and clunky sentences.

Title: The Turn of the Key
Author: Ruth Ware
My Review:
I keep reading books like this (The Silent Patient, The Girl On the Train, etc.) in hopes of finding another Gone Girl, which boasted an electrifying twist, solid writing, and even some social commentary.

Well, Gone Girl this was not—and it might be the last one of its kind I read, until Gillian Flynn writes another book.

The protagonist had zero personality. Somehow, they never do; they're characterized by their paranoia, dread, bad decisions and secrets, etc. It was hard to root for someone I didn't care about.

There were also cliches everywhere you looked, from the lecherous husband, beautiful, slim, distracted wife, hot gardener/chauffeur, protective yet good-hearted caretaker, and bratty teenage daughter.

There was a twist (of course, why else would you read this?) but I wouldn't call it electrifying.

None of this is exactly the book's fault. I'm chalking it up to the genre, which is why I'm giving it a relatively generous three stars.

Title: L'Appart: The Delights and Disasters of Making My Paris Home
Author: David Lebovitz
My Review:
For someone who, on paper, is incredibly fortunate—he lives in Paris with a wonderful partner, has many best-selling cookbooks and an incredibly popular blog, and eats delicious French food and pastries every single day—David Lebovitz sure has some rotten luck.

L'appart is a sometimes amusing, always frustrating tale of Lebovitz's year-long-plus renovation. It's a great window into the French soul as well as a successful anti-tourism campaign. It probably didn't make sense to read this book before his Sweet Life in Paris, because I'm not exactly enthusiastic about a trip to France right now. :)

As others have mentioned, there's a lot of repetition (which always makes me wonder if it was put in deliberately for those who leave a book on their nightstand table and read approximately a chapter a week). I strongly believe you should write for your devoted readers, not your occasional dalliances. But maybe it was unintentional, in which case, that's sloppy editing.

Nonetheless, I still found L'appart revealing and entertaining. If you've lived in France, want to live in France, or live with someone who's lived in France, pick this one up.

Title: On Turpentine Lane
Author: Elinor Lipman
My Review:
I've been on an Elinor Lipman binge lately, and while Turpentine Lane is just as charming, fun, and low-stakes as Lipman's other books, I'm starting to get diminishing returns.

Every book has the same heroine, although the surface details change. She's quirky, funny, close with her family, a little lonely—and she usually lives within close proximity of an attractive man (sometimes he lives with her, as in Turpentine, sometimes he lives across the hall.) I love this heroine, but I'd love to meet another protagonist, too.

I was also uninterested in the house/murder/mystery sub-plot and found myself plodding through those pages.

If this is your first Lipman, you'll enjoy it, but if it's your sixth (ahem), I'd skip it.

Title: Unmarriageable
Author: Soniah Kamal
My Review:
What a charming book! If you're a fan of Pride and Prejudice, you'll appreciate Unmarriageable. All of the recognizable characters and plot points are there, but they've been transformed into Pakistani equivalents. Even the names are refracted versions of Austen's: Elizabeth, Jane, Mary, Kitty, and Lydia Bennet become Alys, Jena, Mari, Qitty, and Lady Binat; Charlotte Lucas becomes Sherry Looclus, etc.

It was fascinating to learn more about modern-day Pakistan, from cultural norms, expectations around marriage and lifestyle, to food, clothes, careers, and more. Soniah Kamal, by way of the heroine Alys, seems to have a complicated relationship with her country: she both loves and is frustrated by it. This is especially clear in Aly's (many) political rants and sassy t-shirts.

While I appreciated the commentary and literary references, Kamal shoehorned Austen references in a few too many times. The transformation would have been more effective if it was subtler. Austen enthusiasts will recognize the clues regardless, and less devoted readers will find the name-dropping tedious.

I also wish Kamal had taken a few more liberties with the text. I felt her trying to stay true to all the pivotal scenes and dialogue, but sometimes it felt like a huge stretch.

These are fairly minor quibbles, and I'd definitely encourage you to read this book book regardless. You should also check out Curtis Sittenfield's Eligible, another fun retelling of Austen's masterpiece.

Author: Jami Attenberg

Title: Billion Dollar Fantasy: The High-Stakes Game Between FanDuel and DraftKings That Upended Sports in America
Author: Albert Chen
My Review:
Rating: 3.5

I have zero interest in sports, let alone fantasy games. But this book fascinated me nonetheless.

It spans the beginning of the (modern) daily fantasy sports landscape to the present, starting with the founding of FanDuel in Scotland and DraftKings in Boston, moving through their early challenges battling each other for market share, then detailing the intense legal and regulatory battles they had to fight with seemingly every state in the country.

The first half of the book is far more enjoyable than the second; I think Chen was most comfortable with the founder-driven narrative, which he had to abandon when he got to the legal stuff. I was most interested in this part of the book, but found myself trudging through it.

Chen also introduces a ton of people, to his detriment. Some minor characters were interesting—I can see why he wanted to include them—but don't add much to the overall picture and ultimately, confuse the reader with an abundance of names and backstories.

Some of the writing is, frankly, lazy. The FanDuel founders are described as the "nerds from Britain" approximately 15 times. The DraftKing founders are meanwhile reduced to "frat boys." While it's helpful to have shorthand for the central groups (especially because we're dealing with a ton of people, as mentioned above), there are subtler, more creative options.

All in all, if you were one of the hundreds of millions of Americans who couldn't watch TV or go to work without seeing an ad for one of these platforms, you're interested in the ascendancy and challenges of a nascent industry, and/or you're waiting for the next Michael Lewis book to come out, give Billion Dollar Fantasy a go.

Title: American Spy
Author: Lauren Wilkinson
My Review:
I struggled to finish American Spy. The lovely cover and unique premise drew me in, but unfortunately, the book was brought down by clunky writing, over-reliance on exposition, and poor pacing.

I didn’t feel like I cared about, or really even knew, the main character. I also didn’t believe her relationships with the other main characters or understand anyone’s primary motivations.

Would give this one a pass.

Title: Such a Fun Age
Author: Kiley Reid
My Review:
Rating: 3.25 stars

Like many other reviewers, I devoured Such a Fun Age. I started reading it around 6 p.m. and didn't put it down until I'd finished at 10.

Feeling compelled to read a book is always great, but I'm less sure if this one passes the mark in other ways: characterization, believability, etc.

There's an intensely detailed yet hard-to-believe subplot involving the main romantic interest, Kelley, and Alix, the protagonist's employer. It felt really, really thin. The more I think about it, the more confused and skeptical I become. Unfortunately, this subplot ends up anchoring the entire book.

The relationship between Kelley and the heroine, Emira, is similarly flimsy. Emira is awesome. We know because Alix is obsessed with her, Alix's daughter Briar is obsessed with her, and Kelley is obsessed with her. Plus Emira has an epic scene early in the book that made me obsessed with her.

But why does Emira like Kelley, who's lame and a little creepy—not to mention sets off Emira's alarm bells several times when they first meet? I'm not sure, because it's never convincingly explained. We just know she feels "adult" around him. Because he lets her stay over at his apartment.

There are several other non-believable relationships and plots I won't go into here, for those who want to read the book regardless. And I would recommend you do: it's sure to be a hot talking point and book club choice. And like I said, I raced through it. Just don't expect a book that holds together when you start reflecting on it.

Title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing: The Only Way to Guarantee Your Fair Share of Stock Market Returns (Little Books. Big Profits)
Author: John C. Bogle
My Review:
3.5 stars.

Halfway through this book (and on vacation, no less!) I dropped what I was doing to navigate through Vanguard's extremely unfriendly interface and buy a low-fee index fund that tracks the market. That is to say: Bogle effectively makes his case.

But as others have pointed out, he makes his case too many times. This book reads extremely defensively, like someone told Bogle you won't believe him unless he proves his point in a thousand slightly different ways, with a thousand slightly different examples. It was too much for me; I started rolling my eyes whenever I could see him leading up to his "misguided investment X" versus the "all-mighty, will-never-fail-you low-cost index fund."

Here's what I'm taking away from The Little Book of Common Sense Investing (which could be littler...):

- Investing is a zero-sum game. If one investor wins, another loses. It's better to own the whole pie than duke it out for slices.
- Reversion to the mean (RTM) means picking a mutual fund based on past experience is foolhardy.
- Reduce as many "unnecessary" investment-related costs as necessary, e.g. sales load, commission fees, buying and selling costs, etc. These costs have a huge impact on your lifetime ROI, thanks to...
- The magic of compounding interest. Okay, I didn't need Bogle to teach me about this, but his premise rests on the investor's ability (both financially and mentally) to buy and hold. In the long run, this leads to $$$$$$.

If you want to be convinced yourself, read this book. If you need a reason to stay away from cryptocurrency, buying and selling individual stocks, trying to predict the next recession, etc., read this book. If you're happy with the summary above and can find your way to a low-cost index fund, skip it.

Title: The Golden State
Author: Lydia Kiesling
My Review:
There are many cliche ways to describe this book—"raw," "unflinchingly honest," "brave," etc., etc.—but that would be a waste, because The Golden State is anything but cliche.

It's written stream-of-consciousness, which is a bold choice, especially since most of Daphne's attention is spent on the mundane aspects of motherhood: feeding her daughter, Honey, entertaining Honey, keeping Honey reasonably clean, and so on. But that's the point. Daphne can't escape motherhood anymore than you can. No book has made me feel so deeply the stuff in between the highs and lows of having a child.

The Golden State also touches on some interesting, timely themes, like Islamophobia, populism, and corruption/bureaucracy/the general uselessness of modern academia. That sounds like a lot, but these ideas are woven in quite deftly. I was surprised to learn this was Kiesling's first novel because it showed a lot of control and maturity.

If you're interested in reading about modern motherhood, I'd recommend this book.

Title: Evvie Drake Starts Over
Author: Linda  Holmes
My Review:
I went into Evvie Drake with fairly low expectations and ended up loving it!

While it's fairly predictable, I didn't mind, because I enjoyed Evvie's personality so much. She's got a great dynamic with the love interest, Dean, as well as the other people in her life (her best friend, Andy; her dead dad; even Andy's girlfriend Monica).

If you're looking for a heartwarming, funny book that has more substance than the average romance, pick this up.

Title: The Grace Year
Author: Kim Liggett
My Review:
Like others, I was excited by The Grace Year's premise. Feminist, dystopian, with a strong-willed character and the promise of a society-wide conspiracy... What's not to like?

Unfortunately, I found myself sprinting through this book just to discover what happened and get it over with. The characters' motivations aren't believable, which makes most of the narrative fall flat. There's also a shoe-horned romance (also not believable) and an extremely bizarre incel sub-plot.

Liggitt managed a few twists, which I appreciated. Nonetheless, there are far better-written books to surprise you.

Title: Missoula: Rape and the Justice System in a College Town
Author: Jon Krakauer
My Review:
4.5

I finished Missoula a couple of days ago, and I can't stop thinking about it. It's a searing account of the "rape crisis" that occured at the University of Montana over four years. (Krakauer cites national campus sexual assault statistics as evidence this wasn't a crisis at all; it's actually on par with average.)

It's non-fiction, but I couldn't put it down. Krakauer does an excellent job dismantling the extremely clever, extremely chilling legal maneuvering 0f the university, the police, and the county attorney's office, not to mention the accused.

The book is clearly sympathetic to the victims (as it should be!) which is a welcome adjustment from the anti-victim bias of what can feel like every authority involved. It made me far more understanding of victims who choose not to report.

All in all, this is a difficult but necessary read. I'd especially recommend it if you've read or are planning to read Chanel Miller's Know Your Name. The legal details are a good complement to Miller's more personal narrative of a sexual assault trial.

Title: The Book of Eating
Author: Adam Platt
My Review:
Platt's an entertaining, self-deprecating writer with wonderful stories. I loved reading about his childhood as the son of diplomat (read: lots of travel, lots of interesting food) and the cast of characters in his family (all opinionated, all eccentric, much like Platt himself).

But this book really calls out for a more heavy-handed editor. I read it in one setting on the plane, which made Platt's over-reliance on certain turns of phrase incredibly obvious and grating.

- Overfed: appears 10 times (first appearance chapter 6, last appearance chapter 21)
- Flowery: appears 6 times (first appearance chapter 1, last appearance chapter 21)
- Dyspeptic: appears 4 times (first appearance chapter 1, last appearance chapter 9)
- Oversized: appears 4 times (first appearance chapter 6, last appearance chapter 21)
- Rabelaisian: appears 2 times (first appearance chapter 3, last appearance chapter 7)

He also hits on the same points over and over again. By the end of the book, I was so tired of hearing about Tom Colicchio's "chef-centric," "radically subversive," "hit" restaurant Craft. Okay, I get it—it was influential! Now let's move on.

Same thing with the DB Burger, which Platt iterates not once but twice is responsible for the "Great Gourmet Chef Burger Craze of 2002," and David Chang's noodle bar, which I'm now well-aware helped spawn the movement of intentional, selective sourcing.

If an editor was on hand to spot this repetition and draw more unique material out of Platt, this could have been a five-star review.

Author: Julie Halpern
My Review:
I read half of this book and then gave up. The premise was good: I liked that the author was exploring depression, a theme typically missing in the YA genre. Unfortunately, Anna is beyond annoying. She's always going off on tangents that did nothing to move the plot forward or add any interest. What's worse, she never stops moaning about how fat she was and how she's a little less fat now.
I could see how Anna was going to make some significant progress with her issues, but I just didn't like her enough to watch it happen.

Title: Where We Belong
Author: Emily Giffin
My Review:
Where We Belong just didn't do it for me. The plot was generic (adopted kid tracks down long-lost parents, begins to love them, folds them into her life and makes "one big happy family.") Vanilla plots can be redeemed by lovable characters, but that didn't really happen here. Marian is immature, weak, and completely overshadowed by all the other characters. Kirby is just okay; I didn't find her very realistic, and I'm exactly her age. Conrad is the one likable character but he's not present nearly enough.
That said, I was glad the ending wasn't completely neat and tidy. Conrad and Marian will probably end up together, but it's left for the reader to imagine their future.
